question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

If the surgeon had operated an hour earlier, (a)/ the patient would have recovered (b)/ without any complications. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• This is a correctly formed third conditional sentence: the if-clause uses the past perfect ("had operated") and the main clause uses "would have" + past participle ("would have recovered"), so no correction is required.

◦ Sentence as given: If the surgeon had operated an hour earlier, the patient would have recovered without any complications.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "If the surgeon had operated an hour earlier," is a properly formed third-conditional if-clause.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the patient would have recovered" is proper, using "would have + past participle".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "without any complications" correctly completes the sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• If she had left on time, she would have caught the flight., If they had saved earlier, they would have bought the house. (third conditional formed correctly needs no correction).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

If the school board had modernised the computer lab several years ago, (a)/ the students in this batch (b)/ wouldn't have struggled so much (c)/ with the new online examination format today. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• This is a mixed conditional: the if-clause refers to a past condition ("had modernised"), but the result described is in the present (signalled by "today"). So the main clause must use "would + base verb", not "would have + past participle": "wouldn't have struggled" must be "wouldn't struggle".

◦ Corrected sentence: If the school board had modernised the computer lab several years ago, the students in this batch wouldn't struggle so much with the new online examination format today.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "If the school board had modernised the computer lab several years ago," is a proper past-perfect if-clause.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the students in this batch" is a proper subject phrase.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "with the new online examination format today" correctly signals a present-time result.

 

NOTE

 

• If I had taken that job offer, I wouldn't have been in this city now. → I wouldn't be in this city now (a past condition with a present-time result needs "would + base", not "would have").

question:

If our national cricket captain had retired right after this World Cup victory, (a)/ millions of his fans across the country (b)/ would be extremely disappointed. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Since the main clause "would be extremely disappointed" is a present-time hypothetical result (not "would have been"), the if-clause must be in the simple past, not the past perfect. So "had retired" must be "retired".

◦ Corrected sentence: If our national cricket captain retired right after this World Cup victory, millions of his fans across the country would be extremely disappointed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "millions of his fans across the country" is a proper subject phrase.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "would be extremely disappointed" is proper, using "would + base verb" for a present hypothetical result.

 

• Option (d) No error — this is incorrect since an error exists in part (a).

 

NOTE

 

• If she had resigned today, her team would be quite upset. → If she resigned today (a present hypothetical result needs a simple-past if-clause, not a past-perfect one).

question:

solution_text:

• After "as if / as though" expressing an unreal or hypothetical comparison, the verb "to be" takes the subjunctive form "were", regardless of the subject. So "as if she is" must be "as if she were".

◦ Corrected sentence: The new intern behaves in the boardroom with such remarkable confidence as if she were a seasoned corporate veteran with decades of experience.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The new intern behaves in the boardroom" is proper, in the simple present.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "with such remarkable confidence" is a proper adverbial phrase.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "with decades of experience" correctly completes the comparison.

 

NOTE

 

• He talks as if he is an expert on the subject. → as if he were an expert ("as if / as though" + subjunctive "were", for an unreal comparison).

◦ Corrected sentence: The urban planning committee proposed that a dedicated cycling lane be constructed along the main arterial roads to ease the traffic congestion that plagues the city every morning.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "along the main arterial roads" is a proper adverbial phrase.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "to ease the traffic congestion" is a proper purpose phrase.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "that plagues the city every morning" correctly completes the sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• The board proposed that the policy is reviewed annually. → the policy be reviewed ("proposed that" + subjunctive base form / "should + base").
